title: The Ordinary Wardrobe
premise: Freya Okonkwo, a translator who has spent thirty years burying her Igbo beneath flawless English, returns to her late mother's flat to sort an ordinary wardrobe and finds it full of clothes sewn from fabric that shouldn't exist—cloth her mother smuggled out of Biafra, each garment stitched with names of the dead. A stranger at the funeral, Adaora, claims to be the daughter of a woman her mother once sheltered, and demands the inheritance be acknowledged publicly. As Freya translates the garments' hidden inscriptions, she uncovers her mother's quiet crimes of survival: debts unpaid, a name borrowed, a life taken in all but law. In the end Freya chooses justice outside the courtroom—she reads the names aloud at a community gathering, surrendering her mother's reputation and her own invisibility, and gives Adaora the one dress that carries her grandmother's name.
about_author: Juniper Coldharbour is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between Lagos and Manchester and writes about the silences families keep to survive. Their work has appeared in small literary journals under three other names they no longer use.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At her mother's sparsely attended funeral, Freya performs grief in perfect English while a stranger, Adaora, watches her too closely and later says her family's forgotten village name aloud. Shaken, Freya retreats to the flat to begin sorting the estate, telling herself she'll be done in a weekend. The emotional beat is denial—the practiced numbness of someone fluent only in endings.

chapters.title: Cloth That Remembers
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Emptying the wardrobe, she finds garments sewn from Biafran relief-cloth, each hem hiding embroidered names in Igbo she can barely read anymore. She begins translating them nightly, and the names start forming a ledger: people sheltered, people betrayed, one entry crossed out with unusual violence. The beat is dread mixed with reluctant tenderness as her mother's voice returns word by word.

chapters.title: What Was Owed
chapters.summary: Alternating Freya and Adaora POVs. Adaora confronts Freya with evidence: her grandmother died after Freya's mother took her identity papers to escape repatriation, and the crossed-out name is hers. Freya, cornered by the truth and by a developer's deadline on the flat, must decide whether to protect the legend or expose the debt. The climax arrives when she burns nothing and hides nothing—she photographs every garment instead.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, closing with Adaora's. At a small gathering in the flat before it's emptied, Freya reads every name from the hems in halting, relearned Igbo—including the confession of what her mother did—and hands Adaora the dress bearing her grandmother's name. Justice happens outside any court: memory itself, made public. The resolution is grief finally spoken properly, and a language, though diminished, no longer dying alone.
